"Instead of disposing of garden prunings through burning or shredding, consider creating a 'dead hedge.' This sustainable practice offers multiple benefits: it provides an excellent windbreak, serves as a haven for various wildlife, and effectively delineates different sections of your garden. To construct one, drive stakes or old fence posts into the ground, forming two parallel rows spaced 50cm apart. Then, begin filling the gap between these rows with your prunings, starting with larger branches at the bottom. As you continue adding material, expect it to naturally compact over time.

Looking for a pick-me-up after a disappointing Christmas? Pre-ordering The Book Of Seeds by Paul Smith, formerly of Kew's Millennium Seed Bank, could be the answer. Priced at £30 and published by Ivy Press in February, this lavish book explores 600 of the planet's most unusual and visually striking plant species. The entries range from a black seed resembling Donald Trump's hair to minuscule orchid seeds the size of pins.

For those seeking winter interest in their gardens, winter-flowering clematis is an exceptional choice. If provided with a sunny, protected location, these plants will generously produce blooms from December through February. Specifically, Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’ and Clematis cirrhosa var. balearica both offer fragrant, creamy flowers with distinctive maroon markings. Clematis cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’ stands out with its pure white blossoms and a more vigorous growth habit. These varieties offer a beautiful and long-lasting display during the colder months."
